ut.title: Ultrasonic Thickness Testing & UT in New Orleans, LA
ut.description: UT inspection in New Orleans for river-corridor piping, tanks, vessels and dock steel: thickness surveys and weld examination to code. Request a UT quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in New Orleans, Louisiana
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes ASNT SNT-TC-1A qualified technicians to New Orleans area sites for ultrasonic thickness testing, corrosion surveys and ultrasonic weld examination. The work usually involves piping, tanks, pressure vessels and structural steel along the Mississippi River corridor, at terminals and at industrial plants. Send the drawings, the governing code and the measurement locations, and we reply within one business day. Request a UT quote for New Orleans.

Why ultrasonic testing matters in the New Orleans area

New Orleans sits on a deepwater river port close to the Gulf of Mexico. Port NOLA describes itself as the only deepwater container port in Louisiana, with six dedicated breakbulk terminals and rail service from six Class I railroads, and Britannica notes that petrochemical plants line the Mississippi above the city. The area is also known for barge traffic, grain and chemical exports, and, at the Michoud Assembly Facility east of the city, large aerospace structures. All of that rests on steel: dock piping, tank farms, loading arms, process lines, vessels, barges and the structures that carry them.

The Gulf Coast climate is hard on steel. Warm, humid air, salt carried inland by storms and long wet seasons keep carbon steel corroding, and low-lying ground keeps equipment in a moist environment. For owners, the question that follows is simple: how much wall is left, and how fast is it going? Ultrasonic thickness testing answers that question without cutting or shutting down a line, which is why it is a routine part of mechanical integrity programs in the region.

What ultrasonic thickness readings reveal and where they mislead

A probe sends a pulse into the wall and the instrument times the echo from the far side, converting it to thickness using the sound velocity of the material. Measured at set locations over time, the readings give a corrosion rate and a remaining life estimate. They also show unexpected behavior: a location that thins faster than its neighbors points to turbulence, a dead leg, or a coating failure nearby.

Several limits apply. Corrosion under insulation is common in humid climates, but a probe cannot read through insulation, so access means removing small windows in the jacketing and insulation and closing them properly afterward. Scale and heavy tuberculation make coupling unstable. Pitting can hide between readings, so suspect areas call for a closer grid or scan. Laminations in plate produce shallow readings that are real reflectors and not a thin wall. And thickness readings do not find surface cracks; for those, magnetic particle testing or penetrant testing is the right tool, as covered on our New Orleans MT page and New Orleans PT page.

Tank farms and terminals deserve a specific mention. On aboveground storage tanks, ultrasonic readings on shell courses, roof plate, nozzles and the annular ring feed the owner's API 653 program, while the owner's inspector decides intervals and fitness. A thickness probe samples only the points it touches, so a floor with extensive pitting needs a broader evaluation strategy chosen by the owner and the inspector. Dock and loading-rack piping, which sees frequent product changes and wet weather, is another place where a routine set of marked points pays for itself over several campaigns.

Ultrasonic weld examination

Weld examination uses an angle-beam shear-wave probe at 45, 60 or 70 degrees, scanned from the weld's sides, with sensitivity set from a reference level or a distance-amplitude curve built on side-drilled holes. The technician looks for lack of fusion, incomplete penetration, cracks and slag, then records each reflector by location, length and amplitude. Acceptance comes from the construction code: a given reflector may pass one document and fail another.

Honest coverage statements matter. Thin wall, tight fillets, nozzle geometry and coarse-grained castings limit what the beam can see. If a weld cannot be fully scanned, the report names the uncovered area instead of implying it was examined. Where a code allows ultrasonic examination in place of radiography, that choice should be agreed with the owner, the engineer and the authorized inspector before work begins.

Codes that govern New Orleans UT work

For new pressure equipment, ASME Section V Article 4 covers ultrasonic examination of welds and Article 5 covers materials, while Article 23 contains SE-797 for contact thickness measurement. ASME Section VIII Division 1 Mandatory Appendix 12 is the ultrasonic examination of welds in vessels. ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.6 describes ultrasonic examination of process piping welds, with acceptance in Table 341.3.2, and ASME B31.1 applies to power piping. AWS D1.1 covers structural steel and its own ultrasonic acceptance criteria for groove welds.

In service, API 510 governs pressure vessels, API 570 governs piping, and API 653 governs aboveground storage tanks, all with the owner's authorized inspector responsible for the program, while Atlantis supplies the thickness and weld data. API 1104 covers pipeline welding, and PHMSA rules in 49 CFR Parts 192 and 195 apply to gas and liquid pipelines. For process facilities, OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(j) requires inspection and testing consistent with recognized and generally accepted good engineering practice. ASTM E797 is the practice for contact thickness measurement and ASTM E164 for contact ultrasonic examination of weldments.

How Louisiana regulates boilers and pressure vessels

Louisiana's boiler law gives the assistant secretary of the Office of State Fire Marshal, Code Enforcement and Building Safety, authority to investigate boiler matters, adopt rules for construction, installation, repair and operation, and issue orders to enforce them. The rules generally follow the ASME boiler construction code, and boilers and pressure vessels that require ASME stamping are inspected under the ASME Code and National Board standards.

That means the state-side record for a vessel or boiler typically comes from a commissioned inspector, not from us. Atlantis does not act as that inspector. What a UT survey contributes is evidence: thickness at agreed locations, mapped and dated, that the owner, the insurer's inspector or the state can read. Ask your inspector what locations and format they want before the job, and put that in the request.

How a thickness survey is performed

The technician calibrates on a step block of matching material, with steps bracketing the expected wall. For corroded or rough surfaces a dual-element probe is the norm because it reads through pitting better than a single crystal. An A-scan view is used so doubled echoes and laminar reflections can be recognized instead of recorded as false thickness. On hot lines in Gulf Coast summer, a high-temperature probe and couplant are required, with the velocity corrected for the surface temperature where the procedure calls for it.

Points are laid out on an isometric or marked on the component, and the same points are re-read in later campaigns so corrosion rate is calculated from like-for-like data. At each point the surface condition is noted, and any reading below the stated minimum is flagged immediately for the owner. Insulation windows are cut, read and resealed, with the sealing method noted so the owner's weather protection stays intact.

Who does the work

Atlantis has no office in New Orleans. Our technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope and are qualified under the company's written practice to ASNT SNT-TC-1A: a Level II performs and interprets, and an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. On Louisiana work the approving Level III is Anoop Rayavarapu, who holds ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Record-keeping follows the written practice, and qualification records can be reviewed by the owner on request. Both ISO 9001 and ISO 14001 certificates are held by Atlantis.

If a terminal, plant or contract requires a specific qualification route, or a procedure approved by your own Level III, say so in the request. It changes the quote and the preparation, and it is much easier to address before travel than on the day.

What the UT report contains

  • Component, line or tank identification with isometric, drawing or CML references.
  • Procedure number and revision, governing code and the acceptance or minimum-thickness criteria.
  • Instrument, probe, couplant, calibration block and calibration check records.
  • Technician name and qualification level, and the Level III who approved the procedure.
  • Thickness tables showing nominal, previous, current and minimum values, with surface and insulation notes.
  • Weld indications with location, length, amplitude, accept or reject, and any uncovered areas.
  • Stated limitations such as temperature, access or coating condition.

Planning a UT job in New Orleans

Summer heat and humidity drive the schedule. Steel in direct sun runs far hotter than the air, so high-temperature probes, shade and early starts matter, and technicians need heat-stress breaks. Rain and thunderstorms can stop outdoor and elevated work quickly, and hurricane season, from June through November, can interrupt any plan, so flexible mobilization dates are sensible. Wet surfaces dilute couplant and make cleaning harder, so dry-off time belongs in the plan.

Site access is the other major factor. River terminals, docks and plants typically require TWIC or site badging, safety orientation and permits for confined space or hot work nearby, and turnaround seasons fill local lodging and contractor capacity. Tell us the facility type, badge requirements, working window and who controls access, and travel and equipment will be planned from that. Mention whether insulation must be removed and who will do it.

Because low ground and levee-protected sites keep water close, some New Orleans plants treat flooding and storm surge as a planning item. After a flood or a major wind event, owners often order a post-event thickness and weld check on exposed piping supports and shell plate. Having baseline readings from earlier campaigns makes that comparison meaningful, which is one more reason to keep the marked-point layout consistent.

UT, MT or PT for your New Orleans job

Use ultrasonic testing for wall thickness and internal weld flaws. Use magnetic particle inspection for surface and near-surface cracks in carbon and low-alloy steel, such as crane welds and repair welds. Use dye penetrant inspection for surface cracks in stainless and other non-magnetic metals, common in chemical service. Many New Orleans scopes combine two or three methods. For background, read the national ultrasonic testing page, the ultrasonic testing guide, the Article 5 thickness requirements explainer, and the Louisiana inspection hub.

Training your own UT technicians

If you would rather build your own team, Atlantis offers UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training, with the ultrasonic testing simulator for practice, plus the ultrasonic testing training overview. Qualification itself is the employer's job under SNT-TC-1A, so supervised experience hours remain necessary. Local details are on the New Orleans NDT training page, and if your written practice needs work, see written practice development.

faq.q: What does a UT thickness survey in New Orleans involve?
faq.a: A technician calibrates on a matching step block, reads thickness at marked locations, records surface condition, and flags any reading below the minimum. The report lists the data in a table that can be compared with earlier campaigns.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing be done through insulation?
faq.a: No. The probe needs bare metal, so small windows are cut in the jacketing and insulation, readings are taken, and the windows are resealed. Agree who will remove and restore insulation before the job.

faq.q: What is the difference between UT thickness testing and UT weld inspection?
faq.a: For thickness, a straight-beam probe measures the remaining wall. Weld inspection uses an angle-beam shear-wave probe to look for internal flaws like lack of fusion, judged against code acceptance criteria.

faq.q: Which code applies to my tank or vessel in Louisiana?
faq.a: In service, API 653 covers aboveground tanks, API 510 covers pressure vessels and API 570 covers piping. Louisiana's boiler rules follow ASME and the National Board, with the State Fire Marshal's office as the authority.

faq.q: How do hurricane season and heat affect scheduling?
faq.a: Storms can halt outdoor and elevated work with little notice, and summer sun heats steel past what standard probes handle. We plan flexible mobilization dates, high-temperature probes and shaded or early work.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have a New Orleans office?
faq.a: No. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope. We quote travel from the job details and do not promise an arrival time before access, badging and scope are confirmed.

faq.q: Can UT replace radiography on pipe welds?
faq.a: In some cases, when the construction code and the owner both permit it. ASME B31.3 and API 1104 contain ultrasonic provisions, but the swap must be agreed with the owner, engineer and authorized inspector before work starts.

faq.q: What access items should I arrange before a New Orleans UT job?
faq.a: Site badging or TWIC, safety orientation, hot-work or confined-space permits, scaffolding or lift access, and removal of insulation windows. Telling us these up front lets us plan travel and equipment accurately.

faq.q: Who qualifies your ultrasonic technicians?
faq.a: Atlantis' written practice, based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, governs qualification, with a Level II performing the exam and an ASNT Level III approving procedures. If your contract requires another scheme, state it in the request.

faq.q: Can my staff learn UT instead of hiring a crew?
faq.a: Yes. UT Level 1 and Level 2 training and a simulator are available. Your employer's written practice sets qualification and the supervised experience hours required before independent work.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Testing (MT) in New Orleans, LA | MPI
mt.description: Mag particle inspection in New Orleans for dock cranes, barge and vessel repair welds, pressure equipment and structural steel. Request an MT quote today.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in New Orleans, Louisiana
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II technicians to New Orleans area sites for magnetic particle inspection of welds, forgings, castings and in-service steel. If the question is whether a crack has opened at a repair weld, a crane attachment, a vessel nozzle or a structural joint, MT answers it in minutes and leaves a visible, photographable record. Send the component, the code and the access details through the quote link and we reply within one business day: request an MT quote for New Orleans.

Where magnetic particle inspection is used around New Orleans

The Mississippi River defines the work. Port NOLA handles containers, breakbulk and heavy lift across a river frontage served by six Class I railroads, and the cranes, spreaders, hooks, lifting beams and rail-mounted equipment that move that cargo carry highly loaded welds. Bulk handling for grain and chemicals adds conveyors, elevator structures and loading equipment, all of them cyclic-load structures where fatigue cracks start at weld toes and attachments. Barge fleeting, repair and fabrication around the river and canals involve welded hull and deck steel, bitts, cleats and tow knees that take shock loads.

Petrochemical plants line the river above the city, and their pressure equipment, structural supports and pipe racks keep repair crews busy with weld repairs that need a surface crack check before release. The Michoud Assembly Facility, built by NASA in 1961, is a reminder that large welded fabrications are also part of the local picture. Wherever welded carbon or low-alloy steel is loaded, vibrated or thermally cycled, MT is the practical surface test.

What MT finds, and the cases where it cannot be used

The method rests on stray flux at a crack. Magnetize a ferromagnetic part, and any crack across the field forces flux out of the surface at the crack. Fine iron particles applied to the surface gather there and form a line that is easy to see. So the part must be ferromagnetic: carbon steel, low-alloy steel and martensitic stainless are suitable, while austenitic stainless, aluminum and bronze, common in chemical and marine service, are not and need liquid penetrant testing instead.

Depth sensitivity is the limit. MT is strongest at the surface, weakens quickly with depth, and does not size a crack. Heavy coatings, wet scale, thick spatter and oil keep particles from moving into place, and Gulf Coast humidity and rain make surface condition a daily concern. MT does not measure thickness; a thinned wall needs ultrasonic testing. Because a crack is detected best when it lies across the field, two field directions are always used.

Equipment and techniques used in the field

The workhorse is the electromagnetic yoke. Under ASME Section V Article 7 an AC yoke must lift at least 10 pounds at the largest pole spacing used, and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke at least 40 pounds, so the technician checks lifting power with a test weight before starting. Prods are an alternative where yoke legs cannot reach, used carefully so they do not burn the surface. Coils and a central conductor are used on shop-sized parts when there is a need for circular or longitudinal fields.

Wet particles in a spray carrier are favored in humid conditions because they stay on the surface and give clear indications on rough weld profiles. Visible particles in a contrasting paint suit daylight work on docks and decks. Fluorescent particles are the most sensitive, but are examined under UV-A light in a darkened area, so a portable tent is used on open sites. A field indicator or a shim confirms that the field is strong enough in the direction needed. On wet days the surface must be dried before particles are applied, or the carrier will not behave.

Codes and acceptance criteria

ASME Section V Article 7 defines the method and ASTM E1444 is the standard practice, with ASTM E709 as the guide. For vessels, ASME Section VIII Division 1 Mandatory Appendix 6 sets methods and acceptance. For piping, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 and Table 341.3.2 apply. For structural steel and cranes, AWS D1.1 and the manufacturer's or owner's lifting-equipment criteria apply, and for pipelines API 1104 and PHMSA rules in 49 CFR Parts 192 and 195 set the framework.

Under API 510, API 570 and API 653 the owner's authorized inspector holds responsibility for the inspection program, and the MT report supports that inspector's decisions. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(j) requires covered process facilities to inspect and test equipment to recognized and generally accepted good engineering practice, which is how many owners justify routine MT on welded repairs.

Bridges and river crossings are a further use of MT in a region full of water. Steel bridge members and connections that fall under state transportation-department specifications are welded and inspected to AWS D1.5, and fatigue-prone details such as cover-plate ends, stiffener welds and attachment toes are the classic places for magnetic particle checks. Elevated steel exposed to salt air and wet weather develops coating breakdown that can hide cracking, so a localized coating removal followed by MT is a common approach when a crack is suspected.

Repair welding adds its own timing questions. On thicker or higher-strength steel, delayed hydrogen cracking can appear hours after a weld cools, so the owner's procedure may require a hold period before final MT. Surface checks are also often done on the gouged groove before welding, between passes on critical joints, and after any post-weld heat treatment. Tell us which stage you need and we will write it into the scope.

Louisiana's state role for pressure equipment

Louisiana law places boilers under the authority of the assistant secretary of the Office of State Fire Marshal, Code Enforcement and Building Safety, who may investigate, adopt rules and issue enforcement orders. The rules follow the ASME boiler construction code in general, and ASME-stamped boilers and pressure vessels must be inspected under the ASME Code and National Board standards.

When a stamped vessel has had a repair, the repair documentation follows the National Board Inspection Code and the owner's quality program, and the MT record becomes part of that package. Atlantis is not the commissioned inspector for the state or an insurer. If you tell us which inspector will accept the work and what they need to see, the MT report can be set up to match.

After the examination: demagnetizing, cleaning and disposition

A magnetized part can attract chips and fines, push a welding arc off course, and disturb nearby instruments. If the procedure or the next operation requires it, the technician demagnetizes with a yoke or coil and confirms with a field meter. Particles and carrier are cleaned off, and marks used to locate indications are recorded.

Indications are first sorted into relevant and non-relevant. A relevant linear indication is measured and compared with the acceptance criteria, marked on the part and photographed. Rejectable indications go to the owner, welding engineer or authorized inspector for disposition, and repaired welds are re-examined with the same procedure.

Who does the work and checks it

Atlantis has no office in New Orleans. Our technicians travel to your site and perform MT under the company's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II sets up equipment, performs the examination and interprets indications, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. For Louisiana MT scopes that Level III is Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. The company's ISO 9001 and ISO 14001 certificates cover its management systems.

SNT-TC-1A is an employer-based recommended practice, so the details belong to the employer. If your contract requires a particular qualification route or a procedure approved by your own Level III, tell us when you ask for the quote.

What the MT report contains

  • Component identification, location, sketch or drawing reference, and date.
  • Procedure number and revision, governing code and acceptance criteria.
  • Yoke or equipment identification and the lifting-power check, plus UV-A and ambient light readings for fluorescent work.
  • Particle type, carrier, surface condition and the technique used.
  • Technician name and level, with the Level III approval.
  • Every relevant indication with position, length and orientation, photographed, with accept or reject.
  • Demagnetization result and any area that could not be examined.

Planning an MT job in New Orleans

Humidity, heat and rain shape every outdoor job here. A damp surface blocks particle movement, so drying time must be built in, and a sudden storm can end the day at an exposed dock or pipe rack. Summer sun can heat steel enough to dry the carrier before indications form, so work shifts to cooler hours or shade. Hurricane season from June through November means mobilization dates need some flexibility.

Docks, plants and terminals typically require site badging or TWIC, orientation and permits for hot work and confined space, and turnaround seasons strain local lodging. MT needs clearance around the weld for the yoke, good lighting and safe access, so scaffolds, lifts and lighting should be arranged beforehand. Tell us the component, surface condition, expected permits and working window, and we plan travel and equipment from that.

Lighting is easy to underestimate on river sites. Visible-particle work needs adequate white light at the surface, and a shaded pipe rack or the underside of a dock deck can be too dark without portable lamps. Glare off wet steel hides faint indications too. We ask about lighting and power at the work location, and bring our own lamps and a light meter, so indications are judged under the conditions the procedure requires and each result can be reproduced by the next inspector.

It also helps to decide who will remove coatings, provide access and give hot-work permits before the technician is sent, since waiting on those items is where most schedule slippage originates on terminal and plant jobs.

MT, PT or UT for your New Orleans job

Choose magnetic particle inspection for surface and near-surface cracks in steel. Choose penetrant testing for non-magnetic metals, or where a yoke cannot be positioned. Choose ultrasonic testing for wall loss and internal weld flaws. A repair on a river-corridor vessel could well use all three. For more depth, see the national magnetic particle testing page, the MT guide, the MT versus PT comparison, and the Louisiana inspection hub.

Training your own MT technicians

If crack checks are a constant need, consider building the skill in-house. Atlantis runs MT Level 1 training, MT Level 2 training and general magnetic particle testing training. Qualification is set by the employer's written practice, so supervised experience hours still apply. See the New Orleans NDT training page and the Article 7 explainer.

faq.q: What can magnetic particle inspection be used on in New Orleans plants?
faq.a: Any ferromagnetic steel: carbon and low-alloy steel welds, castings, forgings, crane parts and structural members. It does not work on austenitic stainless, aluminum or bronze, which need penetrant testing instead.

faq.q: Does MT work in humid, rainy conditions?
faq.a: It can, with care. The surface must be dry and clean for particles to move, so we build drying time into the plan and use wet particles or a tent where weather would otherwise ruin the result.

faq.q: Can MT find cracks below the surface?
faq.a: Only shallow ones. Sensitivity falls quickly with depth, and MT cannot size a crack, so a relevant indication goes to the engineer or authorized inspector for disposition.

faq.q: Is MT used on dock cranes and rigging?
faq.a: Yes, it is a standard crack check for crane booms, hooks, lifting beams and attachment welds on ferromagnetic steel. The scope should state the owner's lifting-equipment program and the criteria that apply.

faq.q: Which acceptance criteria apply to my weld?
faq.a: Those in the governing code, such as ASME Section VIII Appendix 6 for vessels, ASME B31.3 Table 341.3.2 for process piping or AWS D1.1 for structural steel. Name the document in your request.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have a New Orleans office?
faq.a: No. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope, and we quote travel from the job details without promising an arrival time before access and scope are confirmed.

faq.q: Do I need to demagnetize parts after MT?
faq.a: Only when the procedure or the next step requires it, for example before welding or when chips would be a problem. We check residual fields with a meter and demagnetize when necessary.

faq.q: Can paint stay on during MT?
faq.a: Thin, well-bonded coatings can sometimes be examined if the procedure allows, though sensitivity drops. Thick or flaking coatings should be removed locally before the examination.

faq.q: What qualifications do your MT technicians hold?
faq.a: Qualification follows Atlantis' written practice, which is built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, and an ASNT NDT Level III signs off procedures and report review. Tell us if your contract requires another scheme.

faq.q: Can my team learn MT rather than hire a crew?
faq.a: Yes. MT Level 1 and Level 2 training is available, and your company's written practice governs qualification and the experience hours required before independent work.

pt.title: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in New Orleans, LA
pt.description: Dye penetrant inspection in New Orleans for stainless, nickel-alloy and aluminum welds, castings and chemical-service piping. Request a PT quote today.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in New Orleans, Louisiana
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II technicians to New Orleans area sites for liquid penetrant testing, often called dye penetrant inspection or DPI. It reveals cracks, laps, seams and porosity that reach the surface of any non-porous material, including the stainless steels, nickel alloys, aluminum and bronze that magnetic methods cannot test. Send the part, the code and the access details through the quote link, and we reply within one business day: request a PT quote for New Orleans.

Where penetrant testing is used in the New Orleans area

Chemical plants and petrochemical facilities line the Mississippi upriver of the city, and corrosive service pushes owners toward stainless steel and alloy piping, heat exchanger components, valve bodies and vessel internals. Those materials are not magnetic, and welds in them are routinely checked for surface cracks by penetrant testing, both at construction and after repair. Seawater and brackish-water systems at river terminals, cooling water loops and vessel equipment bring copper-nickel, bronze and aluminum into the same category.

Elsewhere in the region, grain and bulk-handling facilities, fabrication shops and barge repair yards use PT on aluminum and stainless fittings, on ground-out repair areas in carbon steel, and on machined parts, shafts and pump components. Michoud, a large aerospace fabrication site on the city's east side, is a reminder that precision welded structure in non-ferrous alloys is also part of the local landscape. Wherever the surface is non-magnetic or the geometry blocks a yoke, penetrant is usually the method.

How penetrant testing works and what it cannot find

A low-viscosity penetrant, red or fluorescent, is applied to a clean dry surface and left to enter any opening by capillary action. The excess is removed and a developer is applied, which draws the penetrant out so the discontinuity appears as a bright line or dot. The bleed-out looks bigger than the flaw, which is part of why the method detects tight cracks.

Limits are straightforward. Only flaws open to the surface can be found. Anything that seals the opening defeats the test: abrasive blasting, grinding, wire-brushing and peening can smear metal across a crack, and paint, rust, oil, scale and spatter fill it. Rough surfaces hold penetrant and give a background that hides small indications. For internal weld flaws or wall loss, ultrasonic testing is required, and on carbon steel magnetic particle inspection is quicker and also picks up shallow subsurface flaws.

Selecting a penetrant system

Penetrants are classified by type (fluorescent or visible) and by removal method. Visible dye penetrants work in daylight, which suits plant and dock settings. Fluorescent penetrants are more sensitive but need UV-A light in a darkened area, so on open sites a tent or a shaded space is set up. Solvent-removable systems are the field standard, requiring only wipes and cleaner, while water-washable and post-emulsifiable systems are used mostly on shop parts.

For austenitic stainless steels, nickel alloys and titanium, the penetrant materials are controlled for sulfur, chlorine and fluorine content so that the test leaves nothing behind that could harm the part in service. In New Orleans chemical service, where chlorides are already a threat, this is not a formality. The procedure should name the lots and certificates of the penetrant materials, and the report should record them. Also plan post-cleaning, since residues in crevices can cause trouble later.

Codes and acceptance criteria

ASME Section V Article 6 defines liquid penetrant examination and ASTM E165 is the general practice. For vessels, ASME Section VIII Division 1 Mandatory Appendix 8 gives methods and acceptance. For process piping, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 and Table 341.3.2 apply. For structural welds AWS D1.1 applies, and stainless fabrications may be governed by AWS D1.6. Many owners add their own limits on indication size or type.

Article 6 gives a standard temperature range of 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for the part and materials. Outside it the procedure has to be qualified at the actual temperature. In service, API 510 and API 570 programs belong to the owner, with the authorized inspector responsible, and the penetrant report supports that person's judgment. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(j) requires covered facilities to inspect equipment to recognized good practice, and PT on weld repairs is one routine way to show it.

Typical components on a river-corridor job make the point. Heat exchanger tube-to-tubesheet welds, nozzle welds in alloy vessels, weld overlay on valve seats and bodies, pump casings and shafts, and stainless instrument tubing are all places where a surface crack matters and magnetic methods are no help. A technician who has done these before knows that tight geometry traps penetrant and developer, so extra cleaning and a second look after the dwell are part of the routine. Where the procedure needs demonstration, a known-flaw comparator block shows the system is detecting what it should at the temperature of the day.

Louisiana pressure equipment oversight

Louisiana's boiler statute gives the assistant secretary of the Office of State Fire Marshal, Code Enforcement and Building Safety, power to investigate, adopt construction and operating rules, and issue enforcement orders. Those rules generally align with the ASME boiler construction code, and boilers and pressure vessels requiring an ASME stamp are inspected under ASME and National Board standards.

For a stamped vessel with a repaired stainless weld, the penetrant record joins the repair documentation under the National Board Inspection Code and the owner's quality program. Atlantis is not the commissioned or state inspector. If you identify who will review the work and what format they want, we write the report to suit.

Step by step: how a penetrant examination runs

  1. Pre-clean with approved solvent or cleaner so the opening is free of oil, grease, paint, rust and scale, avoiding any smearing mechanical method.
  2. Record the part and material temperature and confirm it is within the procedure range.
  3. Apply penetrant by spray, brush or wipe and keep it wet through the specified dwell time.
  4. Remove the excess in the way the procedure requires, without washing penetrant out of a real flaw.
  5. Apply a thin even developer coat and wait for the specified development time.
  6. Examine under adequate white light, or UV-A in a dark area, and evaluate indications against the acceptance criteria.
  7. Post-clean the part, especially stainless and nickel alloys, and write the report.

The skill is in separating relevant indications from false ones such as scratches, weld ripples and trapped liquid. A doubtful indication is wiped away, the area is cleaned and the test is repeated, so the record shows a decision and not a guess.

Who does the work and reviews it

Atlantis has no office in New Orleans. Technicians travel to your site and perform PT under the company's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II performs and interprets the examination, and an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews the report. For New Orleans PT scopes that Level III is Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001 for its management systems.

Chemical-plant owners often have site specifications that go beyond the code, such as contaminant limits or approved material lists. Share them in the request, and we will confirm they fit the work before technicians are mobilized.

What the PT report contains

  • Part or weld identification, material, drawing reference, date and location.
  • Procedure number and revision, governing code and acceptance criteria.
  • Penetrant, remover and developer type, method and lot numbers, with contaminant certificates where required.
  • Surface temperature, cleaning method, dwell and development times.
  • Lighting levels: white light, or UV-A intensity and ambient light for fluorescent systems.
  • Each indication's position, length and type, with photographs and the accept or reject call.
  • Technician name and level, the Level III approval, and any area not examined.

Planning a PT job in New Orleans

New Orleans heat is the main concern. Steel left in the summer sun can climb past 125 degrees Fahrenheit, which dries penetrant before it can enter flaws and falls outside the standard range, so jobs are shifted to early hours, shaded or cooled with wet cloths where the procedure permits. Humidity and sudden rain wet a surface after cleaning and ruin a test, so the surface must be dry and the weather watched. Winter mornings occasionally drop below the 40 degree minimum, which calls for warming the part.

Plants and terminals require badging or TWIC, orientation and permits, and solvent use inside process areas may need approval and fire-watch arrangements. Waste solvent and rags go into the site's waste stream under its rules. Tell us the material, surface condition, location and permit needs, and we plan consumables, tents, travel and schedule from that, with room for weather and hurricane-season delays between June and November.

Pace the job around cleaning. In practice most of the elapsed time in a good penetrant examination is spent on pre-cleaning, dwell and post-cleaning, and not on looking. Owners who agree on a work sequence in advance, with the surface prepared by their own crew and the inspection window defined, tend to get cleaner results and a shorter disruption to operations. Where a plant has solvent restrictions near live equipment, water-washable systems or a cut-out workshop for small parts can solve the problem.

PT, MT or UT for your New Orleans job

Choose penetrant testing for non-magnetic metals or complex geometry, and for surface-breaking cracks of any kind. Choose magnetic particle inspection for steel when speed matters and shallow subsurface flaws are possible. Choose ultrasonic testing for wall thickness or internal weld flaws. Learn more on the national penetrant testing page, the MT versus PT comparison, the Article 6 explainer and the Louisiana inspection hub.

One last note on records: photograph each indication beside a scale and keep the penetrant lot certificates with the report. Chemical-plant owners often ask for those files years later when a part moves or fails, and a clean paper trail is much cheaper to keep than to rebuild.

Training your own PT technicians

If you do a lot of surface testing, you might develop your own staff. Atlantis provides PT Level 1 training, PT Level 2 training and general penetrant testing training, with the penetrant testing simulator for practice. Your employer's written practice governs qualification and experience hours. See the New Orleans NDT training page, and Level III consulting for procedure development.

faq.q: What is liquid penetrant testing used for around New Orleans?
faq.a: It finds surface-breaking cracks, porosity, laps and seams in non-magnetic materials such as stainless steel, nickel alloys and aluminum common in chemical and marine service, and in any non-porous material generally.

faq.q: Can penetrant testing be done on carbon steel?
faq.a: Yes, PT works on carbon steel too. For ferromagnetic steel, magnetic particle inspection is often quicker and also shows shallow subsurface flaws, so we recommend whichever method suits the question.

faq.q: What temperatures can penetrant testing handle?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 6 sets a standard range of 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for the part and materials. New Orleans summer sun can exceed it, so we plan early starts or shade, and record the surface temperature.

faq.q: Why are contaminants a concern with stainless and nickel alloys?
faq.a: Chlorine, fluorine and sulfur in penetrant materials can harm those alloys in service. We use controlled materials, record their lots, and post-clean the part so no harmful residue remains.

faq.q: What happens if it rains during a PT job?
faq.a: A wet surface ruins a test, so the area is dried and cleaned again, or the work waits. We build weather margin into the plan and avoid developing indications in damp conditions.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have a New Orleans lab?
faq.a: No. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope. Travel is quoted from the job details and we do not promise an arrival time before scope and access are confirmed.

faq.q: Visible or fluorescent penetrant: which is used?
faq.a: Visible dye works in daylight and suits docks and plants. Fluorescent is more sensitive but needs UV-A light and darkness. The code, part and site decide which is used.

faq.q: Can penetrant testing be done on painted surfaces?
faq.a: Not through paint. Penetrant needs bare metal open to the surface, so coating must be removed from the test area first, using methods that will not smear metal over a crack.

faq.q: What qualifications do your PT technicians hold?
faq.a: Technicians are qualified under Atlantis' written practice to ASNT SNT-TC-1A, and an ASNT NDT Level III approves procedures and reviews the reports. Say so if your contract names another scheme.

faq.q: Can my staff learn PT instead of hiring a crew?
faq.a: Yes. PT Level 1 and Level 2 training and a simulator are available. Your company's written practice sets qualification and the supervised experience hours required.

rt.title: Radiographic Testing in New Orleans, LA | UT Alternative
rt.description: Atlantis does not perform radiography in the US. For New Orleans welds we can discuss UT, Level III review of existing radiographs, and RT theory training.
rt.h1: Radiographic Testing (RT) in New Orleans, Louisiana
rt.html:
A plain statement first, for anyone who searched for radiographic testing in New Orleans: Atlantis NDT does not perform radiographic testing in the United States. Industrial radiography uses radiation sources that are licensed under U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission rules, 10 CFR Part 34, or the equivalent rules of an Agreement State, and Louisiana is one of those states. Running radiography is not a service Atlantis provides here, and this page explains what we can do for New Orleans owners and contractors instead.

Ultrasonic testing where the code and the owner allow it

Radiography is often written into a specification because the weld needs volumetric coverage, not just a surface check. Ultrasonic testing can supply that on many joints, and Atlantis sends technicians to New Orleans area sites for it: see ultrasonic testing in New Orleans. The decision to swap methods does not belong to us. ASME B31.3 has provisions for ultrasonic examination of production welds, API 1104 provides for ultrasonic examination of pipeline girth welds under stated conditions, AWS D1.1 sets acceptance criteria for ultrasonic testing of groove welds, and ASME Section VIII Division 1 allows ultrasonic examination in place of radiography only in specific circumstances.

For that reason the substitution has to be settled before work starts, with the owner, the design engineer and, on code work, the authorized inspector. Send us the code, joint design, thickness range and the acceptance criteria in the contract, and we will say honestly whether ultrasonic examination fits, what it can and cannot show, and what a procedure demonstration would involve. The two methods give different evidence, and some flaw shapes and joint geometries suit one better than the other.

ASNT Level III review that needs no radiation license

Much of radiographic quality control happens away from the source, at a desk, with images and records in hand. Atlantis founder Anoop Rayavarapu holds ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, and for New Orleans owners and contractors the following review work is possible without handling any source:

  • Independent review of existing radiographs, film or digital images, with their technique sheets, against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code.
  • A second opinion on disputed or marginal indications before a repair or rejection is ordered.
  • Review of a radiography contractor's procedure and written practice against the contract and code.
  • Audit of radiographic records, including image quality indicators, exposure or density records and reader qualification files.

This is consulting from the records. It does not involve exposing a component, and it supports, but does not replace, a licensed radiography contractor. Choosing that contractor remains part of your own procurement.

Radiographic testing theory training

Anyone who wants to understand the method can start with the radiographic testing Level 2 course, which is theory training. Radiation safety instruction and the licensing needed to handle sources are separate and sit with the regulator and licensed providers. Qualification under SNT-TC-1A stays the employer's duty. For classes near you, see the New Orleans NDT training page.

Where to go from here

Tell us what you need to learn about a weld or component: whether volumetric coverage is mandatory, which code governs, and what your inspector will accept. Depending on the answer we will point to ultrasonic testing, magnetic particle inspection or dye penetrant inspection, or to a Level III review if radiographs already exist. Atlantis has no office in New Orleans, technicians travel to the work site for the scope you agree, and we reply within one business day. Ask about UT or a Level III radiograph review in New Orleans.

faq.q: Is radiographic testing available from Atlantis in New Orleans?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiographic testing anywhere in the United States, because industrial radiography needs a radiation license under NRC or Agreement State rules. Ultrasonic testing and Level III review are what we can offer.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing take the place of RT on my pipe welds?
faq.a: Only where the construction code and the owner permit it. ASME B31.3 and API 1104 contain ultrasonic provisions, but the swap must be settled with the owner, engineer and authorized inspector first.

faq.q: Can a Level III review radiographs that a contractor has already shot?
faq.a: Yes. An ASNT Level III can review the images and technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the code, give a second opinion on disputed indications and check the contractor's procedure and records.

faq.q: Where can I study radiographic testing theory?
faq.a: A radiographic testing Level 2 course covers the theory. It does not replace radiation safety training or any license needed to handle sources, and your employer's written practice governs qualification.
